evidence: Field `private readonly yahooFinance = new YahooFinance({ suppressNotices: ['yahooSurvey'] })`: the class creates a third-party HTTP API client itself. This is infrastructure (adapter) work.

getHistorical/getDividends call `this.yahooFinance.chart(...)` with transport-specific options (interval '1d'/'1mo', period1/period2) and map ChartResultArray via convertToHistoricalResult/convertToDividendResult. This is infrastructure (adapter) work.

getQuotes calls `this.yahooFinance.quote(yahooFinanceSymbols)` and, if that fails, falls back to getQuotesWithQuoteSummary, which calls `this.yahooFinance.quoteSummary(symbol)` with Promise.allSettled. This is transport-level resilience logic and belongs in infrastructure.
getHistorical catch block checks `error.message === 'No data found, symbol may be delisted'` to translate the vendor's error message. This is adapter error mapping and belongs in infrastructure.
search() calls `this.yahooFinance.search(query)` and filters on the vendor type SearchQuoteNonYahoo. This is infrastructure (adapter) work.
Class declaration `export class YahooFinanceService implements DataProviderInterface`: this is an adapter implementing a port, placed under src/services (application).
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This file is declared as application layer because it matches the *.service.ts pattern and sits under src/services/**. Its main job, though, is to be an adapter for an external system. YahooFinanceService implements DataProviderInterface (a port) by creating and calling the third-party yahoo-finance2 HTTP client directly. It calls chart, quote, quoteSummary and search on that client. It also maps the library's own types (ChartResultArray, Quote, QuoteSummaryResult, SearchQuoteNonYahoo) into internal response shapes. It handles transport-level failures too: it falls back to quoteSummary when quote fails, and it maps the error message 'No data found, symbol may be delisted' to AssetProfileDelistedError. All of this is transport and adapter work, which belongs in the infrastructure layer (src/adapters/**, src/infrastructure/**). It does not orchestrate a use case, so it is not application work. The file also mixes in some filtering rules, such as which crypto symbols use the base currency and allowing futures only when the symbol is 4 characters long. That shows adapter code and selection policy tangled together, but the main misplacement is that external API access lives in the application layer.

It maps vendor types (ChartResultArray, QuoteSummaryResult) and translates the vendor's 'symbol may be delisted' error message. All of this is transport/adapter work for the infrastructure layer.
